_comment: Curated metadata for Immich 'Art *' albums, keyed by originalFileName (NFC). Joined into the photo manifest by build-photo-manifest.mjs; curation workflow in docs/designs/art-albums.md. 'year' is the display string; 'sortYear' drives chronological ordering; 'facts' are curated now and displayed by a future feature.

A Broad Valley at Sunset - Hippolyte Pet.title: A Broad Valley at Sunset
facts: Petitjean learned the dot-by-dot technique directly from Georges Seurat, applying color in tiny touches the eye blends at a distance.

Almond Blossom - Vincent van GoghFebruar.title: Almond Blossom
facts: Painted as a gift for his newborn nephew, also named Vincent, to hang over the baby's bed.
The branching style borrows openly from Japanese woodblock prints van Gogh collected.

Banks of the Seine at Argenteuil - Édoua.title: Banks of the Seine at Argenteuil
facts: Painted the summer Manet worked side by side with Monet at Argenteuil, the closest he ever came to pure Impressionism.

Banks of the Seine, Vétheuil - Claude Mo.title: Banks of the Seine, Vétheuil
facts: Monet moved to the small village of Vétheuil in 1878 and painted the Seine there more than 150 times.

Boat with Sail (Panormos, Tinos) - Lytra.title: Boat with Sail (Panormos, Tinos)
facts: Lytras painted the harsh Aegean light of his family's island, Tinos, with thick strokes that pushed Greek painting toward Expressionism.

Boulevard Montmartre, Spring - Camille P.title: Boulevard Montmartre, Spring
facts: One of fourteen views of the same boulevard Pissarro painted from a hotel window, tracking the street through seasons and times of day.

Canal of Overschie Paul Signac1906.jpg.title: Canal of Overschie
facts: Signac sailed his own boat to Rotterdam in 1906, painting the Dutch canals in mosaic-like squares of color.

Cliff Walk at Pourville - Claude Monet 1.title: Cliff Walk at Pourville
facts: The two women on the cliff are likely the daughters of Alice Hoschedé, Monet's future wife.
Conservators found Monet scraped out a third figure to open up the view of the sea.

Coffee Table at Lake Starnberg - Wilhelm.title: Coffee Table at Lake Starnberg
facts: Trübner treated everyday subjects with deliberate seriousness, arguing a well-painted table mattered as much as any grand history scene.

Conway Castle, North Wales (1798)-Joseph.title: Conway Castle, North Wales
facts: Turner toured Wales in his early twenties, sketching medieval castles that became some of his first celebrated watercolors.

Dipinto - Sam Francis 1957.jpg.title: Dipinto
facts: Francis began painting while recovering from a plane crash in a body cast, working on canvases propped above his hospital bed.

Dusty Road II - Mihály Munkácsy 1884.jpg.title: Dusty Road II
facts: Hungary's most famous painter of the era, Munkácsy was such a celebrity in Paris that crowds queued around the block for single-painting shows.

Four sunflowers gone to seed - Vincent v.title: Four Sunflowers Gone to Seed
facts: Painted in Paris two years before the famous vase sunflowers - here the flowers lie cut and drying, almost life-size.
Paul Gauguin admired the Paris sunflower studies and traded his own work to own two of them.

Frost at Giverny - Claude Monet 1885.jpg.title: Frost at Giverny
facts: Monet painted outdoors in all weather, once with a hot water bottle and three coats, chasing the pink light that frost gives a field at dawn.

Gardiner's Bay from Sag Harbor - George.title: Gardiner's Bay from Sag Harbor
facts: A teenage work - Bellows was about 17 - painted years before the gritty New York boxing scenes that made him famous.

Grainstacks at Giverny the Evening Sun -.title: Grainstacks at Giverny, the Evening Sun
facts: An early entry in the grainstack obsession that became Monet's famous series - he eventually painted the stacks more than 25 times.
The stacks stood just outside his door at Giverny; he had canvases carried out in a wheelbarrow to catch each light.

Haystacks, end of Summer - Claude Monet.title: Haystacks, End of Summer
facts: From the series that made Monet rich: fifteen were shown together in 1891 and sold out within days.
Kandinsky later said seeing one of these haystacks was the moment he realized painting didn't need a subject.

Helene's Florist Richard Estes1971.jpg.title: Helene's Florist
facts: Estes painted New York storefronts from his own photographs, sharpening reflections until the painting outdoes the photo.
Look closely: every pane of glass carries its own reflected street scene, painted by hand.

Icarus, 1964 © Pollock-Krasner Foundatio.title: Icarus
facts: Krasner painted her boldest large canvases at night during bouts of insomnia after Jackson Pollock's death, working in his old barn studio.

Irises - Vincent van Gogh 1890.jpg.title: Irises
facts: Painted in the asylum garden at Saint-Rémy, where van Gogh called painting 'the lightning conductor for my illness'.
He thought of the irises as studies, but they now rank among his most loved works.

Katsushika Hokusai - The Great Wave.jpg.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
facts: Hokusai was about 70 when he cut this design - he claimed nothing he made before 70 was worth counting.
It's a woodblock print, not a painting: thousands of impressions were sold cheaply, about the price of a bowl of noodles.
Mount Fuji, the real subject of the series, hides in the trough of the wave.

Key West, Hauling Anchor - Winslow Homer.title: Key West, Hauling Anchor
facts: One of the luminous late watercolors Homer made on winter trips to Florida and the Caribbean - he finished some in a single sitting.

La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse - C.title: La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse
facts: Monet was 24, painting the beaches of his Normandy childhood a decade before the word 'Impressionism' existed.

Landscape near Pontoise, the Auvers Road.title: Landscape near Pontoise, the Auvers Road
facts: Pissarro was the only painter to show in all eight Impressionist exhibitions, and mentored both Cézanne and Gauguin around Pontoise.

Mountain Landscape with two Figures at t.title: Mountain Landscape with Two Figures
facts: French-born Legros spent his career in London teaching at the Slade, where he painted entire demonstration pictures in front of his students.

Napoleon at the Great St. Bernard - Jacq.title: Napoleon Crossing the Alps
facts: Pure propaganda: Napoleon actually crossed the pass on a sure-footed mule, not a rearing stallion.
Napoleon refused to sit for it, telling David nobody cares whether portraits are good likenesses.
David's studio produced five versions; Napoleon's name is carved into the rocks beside Hannibal's and Charlemagne's.

Nighthawks - Edward Hopper 1942.jpg.title: Nighthawks
facts: Painted in the weeks right after Pearl Harbor, when New York held nightly blackout drills - the diner glows like the only lit thing in the city.
The diner has no door to the street: the customers are sealed in behind glass.
Hopper's wife Jo posed for the woman in red and named the painting in their ledger.

On the Banks of a River - Paul Cézanneca.title: On the Banks of a River
facts: A late work built from patches of color rather than outlines - the approach Picasso credited when he called Cézanne 'the father of us all'.

Paris Street Rainy Day - Gustave Cailleb.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
facts: The boulevards look new because they were: Haussmann had just rebuilt Paris, and Caillebotte painted the city still feeling unfamiliar to its own residents.
Caillebotte was also the Impressionists' patron - his fortune paid for their exhibitions and bought the Monets and Renoirs now in the Musée d'Orsay.

Poplars on the Epte - Claude Monet 1891..title: Poplars on the Epte
facts: When the township put the trees up for auction mid-series, Monet paid a timber merchant to leave them standing until he finished painting.

Poppies, Isles of Shoals - Childe Hassam.title: Poppies, Isles of Shoals
facts: Painted in poet Celia Thaxter's island garden off the New Hampshire coast, a summer colony for artists and writers.

Regattas at Argenteuil - Claude Monetcir.title: Regattas at Argenteuil
facts: The sailboats' reflections are single broad strokes of pure color - shorthand that scandalized critics used to polished finish.
Monet painted Argenteuil's river scene from a floating studio boat he fitted out himself.

Ricketts Point, Beaumaris - Charles Cond.title: Ricketts Point, Beaumaris
facts: Conder was part of the Heidelberg School, the painters who first captured Australia's harsh sunlight on canvases sometimes no bigger than a cigar-box lid.

Rotterdam - The Steams Paul Signac1906.j.title: Steamboats, Rotterdam
facts: Signac loved working harbors - he sailed to dozens of European ports and painted the smoke, cranes, and steam in confetti-like dabs.

Snow, Boulevard de Clichy, Paris - Paul.title: Snow, Boulevard de Clichy, Paris
facts: Painted the year Signac and Seurat unveiled Pointillism at the final Impressionist exhibition - this snowy street is one of its first tests.

States of Mind Those Who Go - Umberto Bo.title: States of Mind II: Those Who Go
facts: Part of a triptych about a railway station farewell - this panel is the rush of passengers leaving, splintered by speed and slanting lines.
The Futurists wanted to paint motion and noise itself; Boccioni reworked the whole series after seeing Cubism in Paris.

Sunset at Eragny Camille Pissarro1890.jp.title: Sunset at Éragny
facts: Éragny was Pissarro's final home - Monet lent him the money to buy the farmhouse whose meadows fill his late canvases.

The Beach at Fécamp - Gustave Loiseau 18.title: The Beach at Fécamp
facts: Loiseau, a baker's son who took up painting with an inheritance, became known for cross-hatched brushwork he called 'en treillis' - like lattice.

The Channel Sketchbook 29 (ca. 1845)-Jos.title: The Channel Sketchbook, page 29
facts: From a pocket sketchbook Turner carried on Channel crossings in his last decade - sea and sky dissolved to almost pure color.
Turner left more than 30,000 sketches and watercolors to the British nation.

The Channel Sketchbook 48 -Joseph Mallor.title: The Channel Sketchbook, page 48
facts: These late watercolor pages were private experiments never meant for sale - closer to abstraction than anything publicly shown for another 60 years.

The Coming Storm - Winslow Homer 1901.jp.title: The Coming Storm
facts: Homer spent his last decades in a studio on the Maine coast, painting the sea fifty feet from his door in every mood it offered.

The Dogana and Santa Maria della Salute,.title: The Dogana and Santa Maria della Salute, Venice
facts: Turner visited Venice only three times but made it his signature subject, dissolving the city into light on water.
Critics mocked these late Venices as 'soapsuds and whitewash'; Monet and the Impressionists studied them like textbooks.

The Eclipse - Alma Thomas 1970.jpg.title: The Eclipse
facts: Thomas taught junior-high art in Washington for 35 years and began her abstract career in her seventies.
In 2015 she became the first Black woman to have a painting enter the White House collection.

The Houses of Parliament Sunset - Claude.title: The Houses of Parliament, Sunset
facts: Monet painted Parliament from a terrace at St Thomas' Hospital, always at dusk, working on dozens of canvases at once as the light shifted.
He loved London's fog and said without it the city wouldn't be beautiful.

The Little Maure Mountains - Henri-Edmon.title: The Little Maure Mountains
facts: Cross moved to the wild Côte d'Azur for his health and painted it in blocks of violet and gold that pointed straight toward Fauvism - Matisse came to visit and learn.

The Palazzo Ducale - Claude Monet 1908.j.title: The Palazzo Ducale
facts: From Monet's only trip to Venice, at age 68 - he called the city 'too beautiful to paint' and then made 37 canvases.

The Sawmill, December sun - Ester Almqvi.title: The Sawmill, December Sun
facts: One of Sweden's pioneering women modernists; her drawing 'The Meeting' was chosen for the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights stamp.

The Seine - Henry Ossawa Tannerc. 1902.j.title: The Seine
facts: Tanner left American racism for Paris, where he became the first African American painter with international acclaim.
This quiet river view hangs in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

The Seine at Giverny - Claude Monet 1897.title: The Seine at Giverny
facts: For his 'Mornings on the Seine' series Monet rose at 3:30am and rowed out to anchor before first light, painting the same bend day after day.

The Starry Night - Vincent van Gogh 1889.title: The Starry Night
facts: Painted from his asylum room at Saint-Rémy - but from memory and imagination, since he wasn't allowed to paint in his bedroom.
The village is invented; the cypress and swirling sky came from his head, not the window.
Van Gogh considered it a failure and sold not one painting like it in his lifetime.

The Tugboat, Canal in Samois - Paul Sign.title: The Tugboat, Canal in Samois
facts: By 1901 Signac's dots had widened into small bricks of color - he compared the method to mosaics he'd admired in Venice.

The Water Lily Pond in the Evening - Cla.title: The Water Lily Pond in the Evening
facts: Monet dug the pond himself at Giverny and diverted a river branch to feed it, then painted it for thirty years.
Painted while cataracts dimmed his sight - the late pond pictures burn with oranges and purples he partly saw and partly remembered.

The harvest - Vincent van GoghJune 1888.title: The Harvest
facts: Van Gogh painted this view of the Crau plain near Arles in a single furious week of harvest weather and judged it his best landscape yet.
He wrote to Theo that the canvas 'kills all the rest' he had done that summer.

Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji The Great.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
facts: The opening print of the series 'Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji' - the mountain sits tiny and calm in the trough of the wave.
The deep blue is Prussian blue, a pigment newly imported to Japan that helped make the series a sensation.
Debussy kept a copy in his study while composing 'La Mer'.

Two Breton women in a meadow - Émile Ber.title: Two Breton Women in a Meadow
facts: Bernard was barely 20 when he developed Cloisonnism - flat color inside bold outlines, named after enamel work.
He traded paintings with Gauguin at Pont-Aven, and van Gogh kept this canvas's sister work in his collection.

Untitled #21 - Howardena Pindell 1978.jp.title: Untitled #21
facts: Pindell built shimmering surfaces from thousands of hand-punched paper dots, sometimes numbering each one.
She spent 12 years as a MoMA curator while making her own art at night.

Untitled - Alma Thomas 1973.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: Thomas's rhythmic color daubs were inspired by watching wind move through the holly tree outside her Washington window.
She painted her most celebrated work in her 80s, arthritis and all, steadying one arm with the other.

Untitled, 1946 Pollock-Krasner Foundatio.title: Untitled
facts: From Krasner's 'Little Image' period, painted at a table in a small bedroom studio while Pollock worked in the barn.
Critics long filed her under 'Pollock's wife'; retrospectives since the 1980s placed her among the movement's founders.

Venice - Henri-Edmond Crossc. 1903.jpg.title: Venice
facts: Cross anglicized his name from Delacroix to avoid comparison with the famous Romantic painter.

View of Bazincourt, Sunset - Camille Pis.title: View of Bazincourt, Sunset
facts: An eye ailment forced Pissarro to give up painting outdoors in bad weather - many late landscapes were painted through a window, including views toward Bazincourt.

View of a Valley in Normandy - Paul Huet.title: View of a Valley in Normandy
facts: Huet painted outdoors a generation before the Impressionists, helping free French landscape from the studio.

View of the Seine at Herblay (1889) - Pa.title: View of the Seine at Herblay
facts: Painted the summer Signac anchored his boat at Herblay - the calm horizontal dots make the river feel like held breath.

View of İstanbul - Félix Ziem 1821.jpg.title: View of Istanbul
facts: Ziem returned obsessively to Istanbul and Venice, painting golden harbors so popular he became one of the era's wealthiest artists.
He was the first living artist to have a work bought by the Louvre.

Weymouth (ca. 1811)-Joseph Mallord Willi.title: Weymouth
facts: Turner toured the Dorset coast for an engraving series, sketching fishing towns from cliff paths in all weathers.

Wheat Field with Cypresses - Vincent van.title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
facts: Painted near the Saint-Rémy asylum the same summer as The Starry Night - the cypress was, he wrote, 'as beautiful as an Egyptian obelisk'.
He liked the composition so much he painted three versions, one as a gift for his mother and sister.

Wheatfield - Claude Monet 1881.jpg.title: Wheatfield
facts: A decade before the grainstack series, Monet was already drawn to wheat - here as a whole shimmering field under summer wind.

Wheatfield under Thunderclouds - Vincent.title: Wheatfield under Thunderclouds
facts: From his final weeks at Auvers, painted on an unusual double-square canvas - he said these wheat fields expressed 'sadness, extreme loneliness' but also health and strength.

Winter Shadows - Alma Thomasc. 1960.jpg.title: Winter Shadows
facts: A transitional work from the years Thomas was moving from representation toward the pure color abstraction of her famous late style.

study-for-a-sunday-on-la-grande-jatte-ge.title: Study for A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
facts: Seurat made over 60 studies for the final Grande Jatte, hauling his canvas to the island every morning for months.
The finished painting took two years of dots; this oil sketch shows the looser hand he hid in the final work.

Édouard Vuillard - Across the Fields (18.title: Across the Fields
facts: Vuillard belonged to the Nabis ('prophets'), who flattened scenes into decorative patches of pattern and color.

Édouard Vuillard - Square Berlioz (1915).title: Square Berlioz (La Place Vintimille)
facts: Vuillard painted the small Paris square below his apartment window for decades, like a private weather diary.
This view was painted during wartime Paris, the square's calm a quiet act of normalcy.
